justifications.functional_suitability: All requirements are met: Real-Time Scoring Engine scores transactions (R-01), Case Management Backend and UI handle reviews (R-02), and WASM models in In-Memory Scoring Engine alongside Rule Management enable zero-downtime updates (R-03).
justifications.performance_efficiency: Achieves 3,000 TPS under 50 ms via Go/Rust implementation, Payment Ingress ALB, sub-millisecond Redis Cache lookups, WASM in-memory scoring, and asynchronous audit streaming via Messaging Bus (Amazon SQS).
justifications.compatibility: Integrates cleanly with Payment Gateway/Acquirer using standard HTTPS/gRPC over TLS 1.3 mTLS, Core Banking/Card Network Systems, and external Identity Provider using standard OAuth2/OIDC protocols.
justifications.usability: Case Management UI directly addresses Fraud Analysts via Case Queue & Investigation Component and Risk Managers via Rule Management & Audit Component. However, explicit mechanisms for analyst workflow efficiency (e.g. keyboard shortcuts) are unspecified.
justifications.reliability: The Circuit Breaker Fallback Controller ensures scoring failures never block payments over 1 minute (R-07). High availability is reinforced by RDS Read Replicas, SQS DLQs, and managed ElastiCache persistence.
justifications.security: Meets PCI-DSS Level 1: Masking & Sanitization Middleware hides full card numbers, S3 Object Lock and KMS guarantee tamper-evident audit storage, while mTLS, PostgreSQL RLS, and OIDC secure transport and data layers.
justifications.maintainability: Clear container and component boundaries separate scoring, case management, and ingestion. Small-team maintainability is enabled by managed cloud services (ALB, SQS, S3, RDS) and decoupled pluggable WASM scoring modules.
justifications.portability: Tailored for AWS eu-west-1 using standard Docker/container technologies (Go, Node.js, React). Moderate coupling exists to AWS-specific proprietary services (S3 Object Lock, DynamoDB, SQS), but core microservices remain portable.

PERF-01.justification: In-memory WASM scoring, sub-millisecond Redis caching, compiled Go/Rust engine, and asynchronous messaging offload ensure P99 latency remains well under 50 ms at 3,000 TPS.
sensitivity_points: Sub-millisecond latency of Redis feature lookups under heavy concurrency
In-memory execution overhead of WASM scoring modules
tradeoffs: Using in-memory caching increases RAM costs to achieve ultra-low latency

PERF-02.justification: Architectural separation between ingress paths (ALB vs API Gateway) and persistence tiers (Redis for scoring, RDS primary/read replica for cases) prevents analyst workload interference.
sensitivity_points: Independent autoscaling of ingress and compute tiers
Read replica isolation for heavy analyst search queries
tradeoffs: Maintaining distinct compute and database stacks increases infrastructure complexity

AVAIL-01.justification: Circuit breaker mechanisms at both ALB and scoring engine levels enable rapid fallback, though auditing fallback decisions when the engine completely crashes lacks explicit wiring.
sensitivity_points: Circuit breaker timeout threshold and failure detection responsiveness
Persistence mechanism for decisions generated during total scoring engine failure
tradeoffs: Failing open preserves payment flow availability at the cost of fraud risk

AVAIL-02.justification: Asynchronous decoupling via SQS messaging buffers audit records when Audit Storage is slow or down, ensuring zero audit loss and shielding scoring latency from backend storage stalls.
sensitivity_points: SQS retention limits and dead-letter queue monitoring during prolonged outages
Asynchronous decoupling between real-time scoring and persistent storage
tradeoffs: Asynchronous buffering guarantees availability and audit durability over immediate consistency

MOD-01.justification: WASM-based in-memory execution allows dynamic reloading of model binaries without process downtime, while metadata tagging ensures model versions are captured in decision events.
sensitivity_points: Hot-swapping WASM bytecode in runtime memory without request drops
Deterministic model version tagging on all generated scoring decisions
tradeoffs: WASM sandboxing facilitates dynamic reloading at the expense of marginal compute overhead

MOD-02.justification: UI and backend provide rule management components, but the architecture lacks an explicit mechanism or communication channel to propagate updated rules to the scoring engine at runtime.
sensitivity_points: Absence of an event distribution or cache propagation path for rule updates
Consistency of active rules across all scoring engine instances
tradeoffs: Decoupled service boundaries reduce scoring surface area but complicate runtime configuration distribution

SEC-01.justification: Card masking and tokenization middleware prevent analysts from viewing clear-text PANs, but the architecture lacks intrusion detection or anomaly monitoring components to alert within 15 minutes.
sensitivity_points: Enforcement of masking middleware across all analyst API endpoints
Absence of automated threat detection and security alert mechanisms
tradeoffs: Strict payload masking protects sensitive data but limits contextual information during manual reviews

SEC-02.justification: S3 Object Lock with KMS guarantees 7-year tamper resistance, while dedicated DynamoDB query APIs and Report Generator Lambda components enable rapid retrieval and export of decision records.
sensitivity_points: Immutability policies configured via S3 Object Lock compliance mode
Indexing efficiency of historic decision identifiers in DynamoDB
tradeoffs: Dual-tier storage using S3 and DynamoDB balances fast query retrieval with long-term retention costs
